summary:
Paola Estefania opens the workshop (Bereket Habtemeskel absent) by engaging the audience on AI agent security, asking how many give agents access to personal accounts like Gmail. She highlights that agents using user tokens are 'pretending to be us,' analogous to handing CEO credentials to a new hire. She introduces the 'hire your agent' principle: grant agents their own scoped authority, not your credentials. Three core problems are identified: discovery (agents need automatic ways to find services and capabilities), authorization (fine-grained capabilities versus broad OAuth scopes), and traceability (agent identity for audit logs and revocation). Capabilities are more granular than scopes, specifying exact HTTP methods and endpoints. A well-known agent configuration endpoint, inspired by OIDC, lets services publish capabilities. OpenAPI specs can be translated into capabilities as an interim solution while services adopt the protocol.

Paola then explains agent identity through private keys: each agent receives its own key pair, enabling signed tokens and encrypted communication. This shifts the paradigm—agents become principal actors visible in audit logs rather than hiding behind user identities. She introduces the 'host' concept, representing where agents are created, adding another layer of revocation and policy control alongside user and agent identity. Paola discusses the protocol's evolution from V1 to V2, noting the new draft will address enterprise concerns like long-lived versus ephemeral agents and company-level policies, and invites community contributions as open source.

The protocol consists of three layers: an agent plugin for server-side verification and grant issuance, an SDK shipped with MCP support for connecting to Claude or other tools, and a directory matching agent intent to capabilities. A live demo shows an MCP-connected agent reading emails via device flow authentication, requiring capability approval before each new action. The demo demonstrates the full workflow: default read capabilities, requesting approval to send an email via client back-channel authorization, audit logs showing agent ID and user association, and revocation that prevents further access. During closing Q&A, Paola clarifies that the 'proxy' is actually a directory matching intent with capabilities—not a real proxy, which she calls a bad, unscalable idea. She differentiates Agent Auth from AI gateways by emphasizing that agents are treated as principals with their own identities, enabling full lifecycle traceability. She invites the community to contribute via Discord and email.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & Agent Security Awareness
sections.summary: Paola opens the workshop, noting Bereket could not attend. She engages the audience by asking how many use AI agents daily and how many give them access to personal accounts. She highlights that agents acting on behalf of users while 'pretending to be us' is a security problem, drawing an analogy to the early internet era where excitement preceded security concerns.

sections.title: Hire Your Agent Analogy
sections.summary: Paola introduces the 'hire your agent' analogy: when you hire someone, you give them their own credentials, not the CEO's. Similarly, agents should receive their own authority instead of user credentials. She emphasizes granting agents scoped authority rather than full credential access.

sections.title: Three Core Problems: Discovery, Authorization, Traceability
sections.summary: Three problems are identified: discovery (agents need automatic ways to find services and capabilities, like a phone book), authorization (scoping what agents can do at a fine-grained level), and traceability (audit logs showing which agent did what on behalf of which user, requiring agent identity for revocation).

sections.title: Capabilities vs Scopes
sections.summary: Paola explains that capabilities are more granular than OAuth scopes. Instead of a broad 'read' scope, capabilities specify exact actions (GET, DELETE, POST). An agent's intent is matched to specific tool capabilities. She also discusses minting tokens for agents as principal actors rather than for users.

sections.title: Well-known Endpoints & OpenAPI Translation
sections.summary: The protocol proposes a well-known agent configuration endpoint inspired by OIDC, where services publish capabilities and encryption requirements. As an interim solution while services adopt the protocol, OpenAPI specs can be translated into capabilities. Paola attempts a live demo with OpenAI's OpenAPI JSON, then switches to Notion.

sections.title: Directory Demo & Audience Q&A
sections.summary: Paola shows how OpenAPI endpoints are translated into a capabilities directory (e.g., Gmail with ~20 capabilities). The directory functions as a phone book for agents. Audience questions address fine-grained authorization and manual capability configuration, with Paola confirming agents become principal actors with their own tokens.

sections.title: Agent Identity via Private Keys & Host Concept
sections.summary: Paola explains that each agent receives its own private key, enabling signed tokens and encrypted communication. This lets services log which agent performed actions on behalf of which user, shifting agents from hiding behind users to acting as principals. She introduces the 'host' concept—the place where agents are created—adding another revocation and policy layer. Audience questions address revocation (tokens can be revoked via the API) and the fact that agents always remain associated with a user.

sections.title: Protocol Evolution: V1 to V2 & Three Layers
sections.summary: Paola discusses the protocol's evolution from V1 to V2, noting a new draft will address enterprise concerns like long-lived versus ephemeral agents and company-level policies. She describes three layers: an agent plugin for server-side verification and grant issuance, an SDK shipped with MCP support for connecting to Claude or other tools, and a directory matching intent to capabilities. She invites community contributions as the protocol is open source.

sections.title: Live Demo: MCP Email Reading with Capability Approval
sections.summary: Paola demonstrates an MCP-connected agent reading emails using device flow authentication. The agent matches user intent ('bring me my last email') to capabilities from the directory and requests approval. After approval, the agent retrieves emails. Paola shows audit logs with agent ID, user association, and capabilities used. The agent has only read capabilities by default; sending an email requires a separate capability approval via client back-channel authorization.

sections.title: Live Demo: Agent Revocation, Audit Logs & UX Balance
sections.summary: Paola demonstrates revoking an agent's access, then attempting to read emails again—the agent cannot access them. She notes the agent created a new identity but still lacked send capabilities. She shows the full workflow: approve, deny, revoke, and track agent status. Audience questions address time-based constraints and per-action approvals. Paola emphasizes balancing security with UX—using host-level and user-level policies to avoid requiring approval for every action while maintaining safety.

sections.title: Closing Q&A: Directory vs Proxy, AI Gateway Comparison & Community Invitation
sections.summary: Paola clarifies that the 'proxy' is actually a directory matching intent with capabilities, not a real proxy, which she calls a bad and unscalable idea since proxies use data. She explains that future protocol versions will be more locked down so agents can only access services through the Agent Auth protocol. She distinguishes Agent Auth from AI gateways by emphasizing agents are treated as principals with their own identities, enabling full lifecycle traceability—AI gateways do not yet provide this. She reiterates the core message: stop giving agents credentials, give them authority. She invites community contributions via Discord and email, sharing her contact information before closing to applause.
